current_example.title: Example: Reconstructing a Three-Variable Function From Its Gradient

q-81736.name: Question 1
q-81736.worked_solution:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,j.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y)=F(x,y),$ the function $f(x,y)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡y+y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+x
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡y+y)\,\text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡y+xy+g(y)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+x+{g}^{′}(y).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+x$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+x+{g}^{′}(y) & =x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+x \\ {g}^{′}(y) & =0 \\ g(y) & =C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Finally, substituting $g(y)=C$ into our expression for $f(x,y),$ we get

$$
f(x,y)=x\operatorname{sin}⁡y+xy+C.
$$

Find f(x,y) such that ∇f(x,y)=F(x,y), where F(x,y)=(sin⁡y+y) i+(xcos⁡y+x) j.

a
f(x,y)=xsin⁡y+xy+C
b
f(x,y)=x2sin⁡y+x2y+C
c
f(x,y)=cos⁡(xy)+xy+C
d
f(x,y)=sin⁡(xy)+y+C
e
f(x,y)=xcos⁡y+x+C

The gradient of the function f(x,y) is defined as ∇f(x,y)=∂f∂xi+∂f∂yj.

Since ∇f(x,y)=F(x,y), the function f(x,y) must satisfy the following system: ∂f∂x=sin⁡y+y,∂f∂y=xcos⁡y+x

First, we integrate ∂f∂x with respect to x. Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of y: f(x,y)=∫∂f∂xdx=∫(sin⁡y+y)dx=xsin⁡y+xy+g(y)

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to y, we obtain

∂f∂y=xcos⁡y+x+g′(y).

Taking ∂f∂y=xcos⁡y+x into account, we obtain xcos⁡y+x+g′(y)=xcos⁡y+xg′(y)=0g(y)=C, where C is a constant.

Finally, substituting g(y)=C into our expression for f(x,y), we get f(x,y)=xsin⁡y+xy+C.

q-132084.worked_solution:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,j.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y)=F(x,y),$ the function $f(x,y)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡y+3{y}^{2}
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int 2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y+g(y)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}={x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡y+{g}^{′}(y).
$$

Taking  $\frac{∂f}{∂y}={x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡y+3{y}^{2}$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡y+{g}^{′}(y) & ={x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡y+3{y}^{2} \\ {g}^{′}(y) & =3{y}^{2} \\ g(y) & ={y}^{3}+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Finally, substituting $g(y)={y}^{3}+C$ into our expression for $f(x,y),$ we get

$$
f(x,y)={x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y+{y}^{3}+C.
$$

EXPLANATION

The gradient of the function f(x,y) is defined as ∇f(x,y)=∂f∂xi+∂f∂yj.

Since ∇f(x,y)=F(x,y), the function f(x,y) must satisfy the following system: ∂f∂x=2xsin⁡y,∂f∂y=x2cos⁡y+3y2

First, we integrate ∂f∂x with respect to x. Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of y: f(x,y)=∫∂f∂xdx=∫2xsin⁡ydx=x2sin⁡y+g(y)

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to y, we obtain ∂f∂y=x2cos⁡y+g′(y).

Taking ∂f∂y=x2cos⁡y+3y2 into account, we obtain x2cos⁡y+g′(y)=x2cos⁡y+3y2g′(y)=3y2g(y)=y3+C, where C is a constant.

q-132080.name: Question 3
q-132080.worked_solution:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,j.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y)=F(x,y),$ the function $f(x,y)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}={e}^{y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{e}^{y}+2y
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {e}^{y}\,\text{d}x \\  & =x{e}^{y}+g(y)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{e}^{y}+{g}^{′}(y).
$$

Taking  $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{e}^{y}+2y$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}x{e}^{y}+{g}^{′}(y) & =x{e}^{y}+2y \\ {g}^{′}(y) & =2y \\ g(y) & ={y}^{2}+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Finally, substituting $g(y)={y}^{2}+C$ into our expression for $f(x,y),$ we get

$$
f(x,y)=x{e}^{y}+{y}^{2}+C.
$$

Question 3
?

Find f(x,y) such that ∇f=F, where F(x,y)=eyi+(xey+2y)j.

a
f(x,y)=2yey+x2+C
b
f(x,y)=xey+y+C
c
f(x,y)=x2ey+y+C
d
f(x,y)=yey+xy2+C
e
f(x,y)=xey+y2+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The gradient of the function f(x,y) is defined as ∇f(x,y)=∂f∂xi+∂f∂yj.

Since ∇f(x,y)=F(x,y), the function f(x,y) must satisfy the following system: ∂f∂x=ey,∂f∂y=xey+2y

First, we integrate ∂f∂x with respect to x. Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of y: f(x,y)=∫∂f∂xdx=∫eydx=xey+g(y)

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to y, we obtain ∂f∂y=xey+g′(y).

Taking ∂f∂y=xey+2y into account, we obtain xey+g′(y)=xey+2yg′(y)=2yg(y)=y2+C, where C is a constant.

Finally, substituting g(y)=y2+C into our expression for f(x,y), we get f(x,y)=xey+y2+C.

q-37343.name: Question 4
q-37343.worked_solution:
The gradient of the functoin $f(x,y)$ is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\text{ }i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\text{ }j.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $∇f(x,y)=F(x,y),$ the function $f(x,y)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2xy,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int 2xy\,\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{2}y+g(y)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}={x}^{2}+{g}^{′}(y).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}={x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{g}^{′}(y) & ={x}^{2}+3{y}^{2} \\ {g}^{′}(y) & =3{y}^{2} \\ g(y) & ={y}^{3}+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Finally, substituting $g(y)={y}^{3}+C$ into our expression for $f(x,y),$ we get

$$
f(x,y)={x}^{2}y+{y}^{3}+C.
$$

q-37343.html:
Question 4
?

Find f(x,y) such that ∇f=F, where F(x,y)=2xyi+(x2+3y2)j.

a
f(x,y)=x2+y2+3y3+C
b
f(x,y)=x2+3y2+3y2
c
f(x,y)=x2y+y3
d
f(x,y)=x2y+y3+C
e
f(x,y)=2x2+3y+y3
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The gradient of the functoin f(x,y) is defined as ∇f(x,y)=∂f∂x i+∂f∂y j.

Since ∇f(x,y)=F(x,y), the function f(x,y) must satisfy the following system:

∂f∂x=2xy,∂f∂y=x2+3y2

First, we integrate ∂f∂x with respect to x. Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of y:

f(x,y)=∫∂f∂xdx=∫2xydx=x2y+g(y)

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to y, we obtain

∂f∂y=x2+g′(y).

Taking ∂f∂y=x2+3y2 into account, we obtain

x2+g′(y)=x2+3y2g′(y)=3y2g(y)=y3+C,

where C is a constant.

Finally, substituting g(y)=y3+C into our expression for f(x,y), we get

f(x,y)=x2y+y3+C.

q-124731.name: Question 5
q-124731.worked_solution:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y,z)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,j+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\,k.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z),$ the function $f(x,y,z)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x+y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2y+x+z,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=y-2z
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y$ and $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (2x+y)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{2}+xy+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x+\frac{∂g}{∂y}
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2y+x+z$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}x+\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =2y+x+z \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =2y+z\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate $\frac{∂g}{∂y}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z) & =\int \frac{∂g}{∂y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\int (2y+z)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={y}^{2}+yz+h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z)={y}^{2}+yz+h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x,y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+xy+{y}^{2}+yz+h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂z}=y+{h}^{′}(z).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂z}=y-2z$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}y-2z & =y+{h}^{′}(z) \\ {h}^{′}(z) & =-2z \\ h(z) & =-{z}^{2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently,

$$
f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+xy+{y}^{2}+yz-{z}^{2}+C.
$$

?

Find f(x,y,z) such that ∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z), where F(x,y,z)=(2x+y)i+(2y+x+z)j+(y−2z)k.

a
 f(x,y,z)=x2+xy+y2+yz−z2+C
b
 f(x,y,z)=x2+y2−2xz2+C
c
 f(x,y,z)=xy−y2+2yz+z2+C
d
 f(x,y,z)=x2y−xy+xy2z2+C
e
 f(x,y,z)=x2+zy2−yz2+C
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The gradient of the function f(x,y,z) is defined as ∇f(x,y,z)=∂f∂xi+∂f∂yj+∂f∂zk.

Since ∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z), the function f(x,y,z) must satisfy the following system: ∂f∂x=2x+y,∂f∂y=2y+x+z,∂f∂z=y−2z

First, we integrate ∂f∂x with respect to x. Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of y and z: f(x,y,z)=∫∂f∂xdx=∫(2x+y)dx=x2+xy+g(y,z)

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to y, we obtain ∂f∂y=x+∂g∂y

Taking ∂f∂y=2y+x+z into account, we obtain

x+∂g∂y=2y+x+z∂g∂y=2y+z

Now, we integrate ∂g∂y with respect to y. Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of z: g(y,z)=∫∂g∂ydy=∫(2y+z)dy=y2+yz+h(z)

Substituting g(y,z)=y2+yz+h(z) in the expression for f(x,y,z), we get f(x,y,z)=x2+xy+y2+yz+h(z).

To determine the function h(z), we differentiate f(x,y,z) with respect to z. This gives ∂f∂z=y+h′(z).

Taking ∂f∂z=y−2z into account, we obtain y−2z=y+h′(z)h′(z)=−2zh(z)=−z2+C.

Consequently, f(x,y,z)=x2+xy+y2+yz−z2+C.

q-81741.name: Question 6
q-81741.problem:
Consider the function

$$
F(x,y,z)=y{e}^{xy}\,i+x{e}^{xy}\,j+3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3z)\,k.
$$

Find $f(x,y,z)$ such that $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z).$
q-81741.worked_solution:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y,z)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{i}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,\text{j}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\,\text{k}.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z),$ the function $f(x,y,z)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=y{e}^{xy},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{e}^{xy},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3z)
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y$ and $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int y{e}^{xy}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{xy}+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{e}^{xy}+\frac{∂g}{∂y}
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{e}^{xy}$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}x{e}^{xy}+\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =x{e}^{xy} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now we integrate $\frac{∂g}{∂y}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z) & =\int \frac{∂g}{∂y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\int 0\,\text{d}y \\  & =h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z)=h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x,y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z)={e}^{xy}+h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂z}={h}^{′}(z).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂z}=3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3z)$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{′}(z) & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3z) \\ h(z) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(3z)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Consequently,

$$
f(x,y,z)={e}^{xy}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3z)+C.
$$

q-81741.html:
Question 6
?

Consider the function F(x,y,z)=yexyi+xexyj+3cos⁡(3z)k. Find f(x,y,z) such that ∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z).

a
f(x,y,z)=exy+sin⁡(3z)+C
b
f(x,y,z)=yexy+3cos⁡(3z)+C
c
f(x,y,z)=(x+y)exy+cos⁡(3z)+C
d
f(x,y,z)=xexy+3sin⁡(3z)+C
e
f(x,y,z)=exy+cos⁡(3z)+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The gradient of the function f(x,y,z) is defined as ∇f(x,y,z)=∂f∂xi+∂f∂yj+∂f∂zk.

Since ∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z), the function f(x,y,z) must satisfy the following system: ∂f∂x=yexy,∂f∂y=xexy,∂f∂z=3cos⁡(3z)

First, we integrate ∂f∂x with respect to x. Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of y and z: f(x,y,z)=∫∂f∂xdx=∫yexydx=exy+g(y,z)

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to y, we obtain ∂f∂y=xexy+∂g∂y

Taking ∂f∂y=xexy into account, we obtain xexy+∂g∂y=xexy∂g∂y=0

Now we integrate ∂g∂y with respect to y. Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of z: g(y,z)=∫∂g∂ydy=∫0dy=h(z)

Substituting g(y,z)=h(z) in the expression for f(x,y,z), we get f(x,y,z)=exy+h(z).

To determine the function h(z), we differentiate f(x,y,z) with respect to z. This gives ∂f∂z=h′(z).

Taking ∂f∂z=3cos⁡(3z) into account, we obtain h′(z)=3cos⁡(3z)h(z)=sin⁡(3z)+C, where C is a constant.

Consequently, f(x,y,z)=exy+sin⁡(3z)+C.

q-81739.name: Question 7
q-81739.worked_solution:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y,z)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,j+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\,k.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z),$ the function $f(x,y,z)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡z+y\operatorname{cos}⁡x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=-x\operatorname{sin}⁡z
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y$ and $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\operatorname{cos}⁡z+y\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{cos}⁡z+y\operatorname{sin}⁡x+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\frac{∂g}{∂y}
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate $\frac{∂g}{∂y}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z) & =\int \frac{∂g}{∂y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\int 0\,\text{d}y \\  & =h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z)=h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x,y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z)=x\operatorname{cos}⁡z+y\operatorname{sin}⁡x+h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂z}=-x\operatorname{sin}⁡z+{h}^{′}(z).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂z}=-x\operatorname{sin}⁡z$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}-x\operatorname{sin}⁡z & =-x\operatorname{sin}⁡z+{h}^{′}(z) \\ {h}^{′}(z) & =0 \\ h(z) & =C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Consequently,

$$
f(x,y,z)=x\operatorname{cos}⁡z+y\operatorname{sin}⁡x+C.
$$

Since ∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z), the function f(x,y,z) must satisfy the following system: ∂f∂x=cos⁡z+ycos⁡x,∂f∂y=sin⁡x,∂f∂z=−xsin⁡z

First, we integrate ∂f∂x with respect to x. Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of y and z: f(x,y,z)=∫∂f∂xdx=∫(cos⁡z+ycos⁡x)dx=xcos⁡z+ysin⁡x+g(y,z)

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to y, we obtain ∂f∂y=sin⁡x+∂g∂y

Taking ∂f∂y=sin⁡x into account, we obtain

sin⁡x+∂g∂y=sin⁡x∂g∂y=0

Now, we integrate ∂g∂y with respect to y. Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of z: g(y,z)=∫∂g∂ydy=∫0dy=h(z)

Taking ∂f∂z=−xsin⁡z into account, we obtain −xsin⁡z=−xsin⁡z+h′(z)h′(z)=0h(z)=C, where C is a constant.

q-81752.name: Question 8
q-81752.problem:
Consider the function

$$
F(x,y,z)=(yz{e}^{xz}+z)\,i+({e}^{xz}+1)\,j+(xy{e}^{xz}+x)\,k.
$$

Find $f(x,y,z)$ such that $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z).$
q-81752.worked_solution:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y,z)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{i}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,\text{j}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\,\text{k}.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z),$ the function $f(x,y,z)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=yz{e}^{xz}+z,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={e}^{xz}+1,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=xy{e}^{xz}+x
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y$ and $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (yz{e}^{xz}+z)\,\text{d}x \\  & =y{e}^{xz}+xz+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}={e}^{xz}+\frac{∂g}{∂y}
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}={e}^{xz}+1$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{xz}+\frac{∂g}{∂y} & ={e}^{xz}+1 \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Now we integrate $\frac{∂g}{∂y}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z) & =\int \frac{∂g}{∂y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\int 1\,\text{d}y \\  & =y+h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z)=y+h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x,y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z)=y{e}^{xz}+xz+y+h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂z}=xy{e}^{xz}+x+{h}^{′}(z).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂z}=xy{e}^{xz}+x$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}xy{e}^{xz}+x+{h}^{′}(z) & =zy{e}^{xz}+x \\ {h}^{′}(z) & =0 \\ h(z) & =C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Consequently,

$$
f(x,y,z)=y{e}^{xz}+xz+y+C.
$$

Question 8
?

Consider the function F(x,y,z)=(yzexz+z)i+(exz+1)j+(xyexz+x)k. Find f(x,y,z) such that ∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z).

a
f(x,y,z)=xzexz+y+C
b
f(x,y,z)=yexz+yz+x+C
c
f(x,y,z)=xzexz+xz+C
d
f(x,y,z)=yexz+xz+y+C
e
f(x,y,z)=yexz+xy+z+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The gradient of the function f(x,y,z) is defined as ∇f(x,y,z)=∂f∂xi+∂f∂yj+∂f∂zk.

Since ∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z), the function f(x,y,z) must satisfy the following system: ∂f∂x=yzexz+z,∂f∂y=exz+1,∂f∂z=xyexz+x

First, we integrate ∂f∂x with respect to x. Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of y and z: f(x,y,z)=∫∂f∂xdx=∫(yzexz+z)dx=yexz+xz+g(y,z)

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to y, we obtain ∂f∂y=exz+∂g∂y

Taking ∂f∂y=exz+1 into account, we obtain exz+∂g∂y=exz+1∂g∂y=1

Now we integrate ∂g∂y with respect to y. Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of z: g(y,z)=∫∂g∂ydy=∫1dy=y+h(z)

Substituting g(y,z)=y+h(z) in the expression for f(x,y,z), we get f(x,y,z)=yexz+xz+y+h(z).

To determine the function h(z), we differentiate f(x,y,z) with respect to z. This gives ∂f∂z=xyexz+x+h′(z).

Taking ∂f∂z=xyexz+x into account, we obtain xyexz+x+h′(z)=zyexz+xh′(z)=0h(z)=C, where C is a constant.

Consequently, f(x,y,z)=yexz+xz+y+C.

q-81755.name: Question 9
q-81755.problem:
Consider the function

$$
F(x,y,z)=2x{y}^{3}z\,i+(3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}z+{z}^{2})\,j+({x}^{2}{y}^{3}+2yz)\,k.
$$

Find $f(x,y,z)$ such that $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z).$
q-81755.worked_solution:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y,z)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{i}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,\text{j}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\,\text{k}.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z),$ the function $f(x,y,z)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x{y}^{3}z,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}z+{z}^{2},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}={x}^{2}{y}^{3}+2yz
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y$ and $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int 2x{y}^{3}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{2}{y}^{3}z+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}z+\frac{∂g}{∂y}
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}z+{z}^{2}$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}z+\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}z+{z}^{2} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & ={z}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now we integrate $\frac{∂g}{∂y}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z) & =\int \frac{∂g}{∂y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\int {z}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =y{z}^{2}+h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z)=y{z}^{2}+h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x,y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}{y}^{3}z+y{z}^{2}+h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂z}={x}^{2}{y}^{3}+2yz+{h}^{′}(z).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂z}={x}^{2}{y}^{3}+2yz$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}{y}^{3}+2yz+{h}^{′}(z) & ={x}^{2}{y}^{3}+2yz \\ {h}^{′}(z) & =0 \\ h(z) & =C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Consequently,

$$
f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}{y}^{3}z+y{z}^{2}+C.
$$

Question 9
?

Consider the function F(x,y,z)=2xy3zi+(3x2y2z+z2)j+(x2y3+2yz)k. Find f(x,y,z) such that ∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z).

a
f(x,y,z)=x2y3z+yz2+C
b
f(x,y,z)=x2yz+y+z+C
c
f(x,y,z)=2x2y2z+yz+C
d
f(x,y,z)=x2y2z+2yz+C
e
f(x,y,z)=3x2y2z+2yz2+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The gradient of the function f(x,y,z) is defined as ∇f(x,y,z)=∂f∂xi+∂f∂yj+∂f∂zk.

Since ∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z), the function f(x,y,z) must satisfy the following system: ∂f∂x=2xy3z,∂f∂y=3x2y2z+z2,∂f∂z=x2y3+2yz

First, we integrate ∂f∂x with respect to x. Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of y and z: f(x,y,z)=∫∂f∂xdx=∫2xy3zdx=x2y3z+g(y,z)

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to y, we obtain ∂f∂y=3x2y2z+∂g∂y

Taking ∂f∂y=3x2y2z+z2 into account, we obtain 3x2y2z+∂g∂y=3x2y2z+z2∂g∂y=z2

Now we integrate ∂g∂y with respect to y. Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of z: g(y,z)=∫∂g∂ydy=∫z2dy=yz2+h(z)

Substituting g(y,z)=yz2+h(z) in the expression for f(x,y,z), we get f(x,y,z)=x2y3z+yz2+h(z).

To determine the function h(z), we differentiate f(x,y,z) with respect to z. This gives ∂f∂z=x2y3+2yz+h′(z).

Taking ∂f∂z=x2y3+2yz into account, we obtain x2y3+2yz+h′(z)=x2y3+2yzh′(z)=0h(z)=C, where C is a constant.

Consequently, f(x,y,z)=x2y3z+yz2+C.
